Industry observers note that in this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Most of the deals we outline below can be found at Backcountry, at REI, and at specific manufacturers like Black Diamond.

Backcountry released its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

On the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:.

According to recent reports, looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

Sources indicate that real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need latest shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you plan ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

If your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

La Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

It has been revealed that with great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

We haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers big-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a big downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s massive toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Update: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

It has been revealed that beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

According to recent reports, most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

It has been revealed that we tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re substantial fans.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

It has been revealed that A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

One of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After swiftly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

Industry observers note that one of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

After swiftly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

#125875. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).
  • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.
  • Sources indicate that the GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

Sources indicate that the GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

According to recent reports, “On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

Sources indicate that AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

Located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

According to recent reports, because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

According to recent reports, “If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard said. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

It has been revealed that batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard said he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

“They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard stated. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Fresh Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Important Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
  • The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
  • Recent findings suggest that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Recent findings suggest that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

Chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The new rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

The charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

It has been revealed that adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” says Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

Industry observers note that “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain users, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” indicates Rodrigues. “That remarked, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

The charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

Industry observers note that I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential newly introduced rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

The TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” states Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

Under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

The charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” says Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

It has been revealed that nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret says the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

Sources indicate that the variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” says Perret.

“The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she notes, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you swiftly and swiftly out of it.”.

According to recent reports, day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he claims. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

Multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the manufacturer Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

Recent findings suggest that I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any problem. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these fresh rules for 2027.

One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

Sources indicate that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the substantial monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

#125873. Tech Report: What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)

Tech Report: What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah.
  • Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting.
  • Recent findings suggest that have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

Recent findings suggest that have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

Intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

In a recent development, while no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a latest book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

“We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson indicates.

In a recent development, after giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

It has been revealed that most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

In a recent development, some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

Others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber stated they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

With all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson says. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

“While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson says.

So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

Sources indicate that most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

Sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

It has been revealed that “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

Sources indicate that then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

Next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

It has been revealed that most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson says it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

An notable thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

According to recent reports, what if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson says to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

Recent findings suggest that since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

Sources indicate that with distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

Sources indicate that in the case of eustress, Robertson claims you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

To seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson states. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

According to recent reports, parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.

  • Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) noted in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A helicopter transports a deceased hiker recovered from Humboldt Peak. (Photo: Custer County Sheriff's Office).

A hiker who went missing on a Colorado 14er earlier this week was found dead from an apparent fall on November 24, following a three-day search that sent rescuers combing the high country in winter conditions.

Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) noted in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.

Sources indicate that authorities stated that the hiker had summited 14,068-foot Humboldt Peak solo early on the morning of Sunday, November 22. At 5 p.m., CCSAR was notified that the hiker still hadn’t returned, and sent teams into the field alongside aerial support from Reach Air and Flight for Life. The missing hiker had shared his plan with his family; however, while rescuers quickly located his car, they were unable to locate him despite searching through the night in winter weather. Additional ground teams joined the search the following morning, but fared no better.

Industry observers note that after pausing the search for the night, 21 volunteers, including K9 teams and drone operators, returned to the field on Tuesday. During the operation, authorities closed the South Colony area to cars and hikers.

In a statement, the Custer County Sheriff’s Office offered its condolences to the deceased hiker’s family, friends, and fiancé, and noted that both the hiker’s plan and cell phone forensics helped authorities determine where they should look.

In a recent development, compared to other 14ers in the same area, the hike up Humboldt is relatively straightforward. The standard West Ridge route follows the feature of the same name roughly 11 miles out and back to the summit. During fall and winter, however, snow and ice can both make it more difficult to stay on-route and increase the consequences of a slip on the peak’s exposed ridgeline. It was not immediately clear which route the hiker took to the summit.

The nearby South Colony SNOTEL station, which sits at 10,800 feet, recorded 16 inches of snow on the ground on November 22, up nearly 7 inches from the week prior.

#125867. I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.
  • That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.
  • Sources indicate that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge).

“How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.

That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

Sources indicate that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

Recent findings suggest that fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

I was 52, the age when menopause, graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something significant to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from the beach, I bought a hooded, five-millimeter wetsuit and booties, and started surfing several mornings a week, collecting phone numbers of women I met in the lineup and parking lot.

After decades of giving everything I had to everyone around me—work colleagues, kids, husband, dogs, parents, sisters—surfing was just for me.

Soon I had built a community of women surfers aged 25 to 75 to join me for dawn patrol sessions at our break north of San Francisco and surf trips to Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, San Diego, and Santa Cruz.

Surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

Seeking guidance on how to surf through surgery recovery and treatment, I posted a message on the Facebook “Women Who Surf” group of 39,000: “I just got diagnosed with breast cancer and am looking for other women surfers who surfed through chemo, and surfed after a double mastectomy.”.

It has been revealed that A hundred women weighed in with personal experience of cancer and surfing. Most hadn’t surfed during surgery recovery or chemotherapy due to doctors’ orders, infection risk, weak immune systems, limited mobility, fatigue, and weakness.

It has been revealed that but one woman told me to go for it: Melanie Ezell, a 42-year-old significant wave surfer, based in Oahu, who surfed through ovarian cancer. She became my role model, inspiring me to paddle out as soon as I could.

It has been revealed that that long-awaited day came after being grounded on land for seven weeks following my double mastectomy. It was three days after my first chemotherapy infusion when my plastic surgeon declared my chest incisions adequately healed. I drove immediately to the beach, paddled out, and felt triumphant when I caught my first wave of the session.

And I kept paddling out through the remaining 11 rounds of chemotherapy.

On days when the swell was big and I was weak with fatigue, I’d claw through the impact zone after riding a wave, leaving my arms drained of power and lungs gasping for air. Once safely outside breaking waves, I’d rest on my board and let sets roll past until my breathing slowed. Still, being in the ocean felt like an antidote to the toxic drugs coursing through my veins. I loved watching the birds and seals, scanning the horizon for incoming sets, paddling into a rising wave, feeling its energy connect with my board.

In a recent development, sometimes those sessions lasted only an hour because of my reduced stamina. But they always left me feeling stoked and alive, adjectives easily lost when you spend Tuesday afternoons hooked up to an IV bag pumping the sledgehammer drug Taxol into a port in your chest.

After my last chemotherapy session, I started ten rounds of targeted immunotherapy infusions (which I just concluded this month) and began posting GoPro videos on Instagram and Facebook of me surfing bald to inspire other women. I wanted them to see what it looks like when breast cancer takes your breasts and hair, but not your identity.

Women from around the world reached out to share their own stories: Ellen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old massage therapist and mom surfing through rectal cancer in the chilly waters at the Oregon-California border; 32-year-old Lottie Bakewell from Cornwall, England, surfing through breast cancer and the demands of caring for her one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter; Belen Kimble, a 48-year-old former professional longboarder, World Surf League commentator, surf performance coach, and single mom in New South Wales, Australia, surfing through breast cancer; and Caroline Wilhelm, a 55-year-old surfer and competitor from Los Angeles who took my cue to keep surfing through her breast cancer.

Backed by growing research showing that physical activity during cancer treatment offsets chemotherapy side effects and improves recovery and resilience, my little cohort of surfing cancer patients proves the ocean is not just a sanctuary, but an active prescription for healing.

But you don’t have to be a surfer to reap the benefits of physical activity during cancer. A upcoming study of 45,530 women published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in September 2026 confirmed what my surf sisters and I already knew: regular exercise gives women going through breast cancer the strength to bounce back more fully and reclaim our lives after treatment. The study followed women for 15 years with data from the Women’s Health Initiative and found that keeping up physical activity and healthy habits prior to a cancer diagnosis acts as a powerful buffer against the physical toll of cancer treatments.

The trick is to start with small amounts of exercise and work with your care team on a game plan to get active.

It has been revealed that “Even if you are not an exerciser, you can still start an exercise regimen during chemotherapy,” remarked my oncologist Eva Thomas, MD, from Kaiser Permanente Oakland in California, who encouraged and cheered on my surfing during chemotherapy. “It sounds counter-intuitive, but women tell me that when they push themselves to exercise, they feel better. Mood is better, sleep is better, energy is increased, and body aches are reduced.”.

It has been revealed that in 2022, the American Society of Clinical Oncology released the first-ever exercise guidelines based on more than 100 clinical trials examining the link between exercise and cancer treatment. For anyone going through cancer who wants to get active, the American College of Sports Medicine created a step-by-step guide in 2024 with research benefits and resources. It outlines a path to get started.

My own path began years before cancer, as a young woman fixated on surfing, who waited decades to act upon her dream.

Industry observers note that looking back, I see that my surfing community—and the strength and identity it gave me—helped me to charge forward through the scariest chapter of my life. The takeaway lesson is useful for all women and men facing challenges: Don’t delay trying something upcoming and scary. It may end up transforming, and saving, you.

Recent findings suggest that danielle Cass lives with her husband in Northern California, where they raised their 26-year-old son, 23-year-old daughter, and dogs. When she’s not surfing with friends, she leads Responsible AI enablement at Microsoft. A two-minute short film about her midlife entry into surfing Learning to Surf at 52 screened at the 2022 San Diego Surf Festival. Follow her surfing through cancer adventures on Instagram @danielle.cass and Substack Danielle Rides the Cancer Wave.

A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
  • According to recent reports, in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
  • In a recent development, like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

According to recent reports, in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

In a recent development, like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

“To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) launched a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

“People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett mentioned.

It has been revealed that as part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

Industry observers note that “You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett said. “Just take pictures.”.

Nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett notes enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

“For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett said.

Industry observers note that kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people blueprint their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

“We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

It has been revealed that the map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that reveals the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

The tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as Newly introduced Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

BLM’s new map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

Gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

“Trails are kind of living things,” Ray noted. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

Move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray noted.

“If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she said. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

For trail users like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she notes, it never will.

Sources indicate that “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett claims. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

In a recent development, she added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

Industry observers note that “Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett remarked. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

#125861. Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (935 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors.
  • Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer.
  • I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors. (Photo: Courtesy Falkenstein Family Collection).

Chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer. Better known by many as Falky, Finkelstein, Steiny, Schwackenstein, or Commando, Chris wore many hats throughout his life: devoted husband and father, loyal friend, accomplished climber, photographer, skier, whitewater kayaker, windsurfer, mountain biker, self-proclaimed computer nerd, and passionate lover of Yosemite and the outdoors.

I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport. I enjoyed it, but pursued other sports. In a way, I don’t think I’ve found a climbing partner that was ever as dialed as he was. My Dad was so quiet and humble about his achievements; there were so many things he never mentioned. I remember being out climbing with him, when he would tell some story like, “We were out here in the ‘80s, blasting a boom box and climbing.” It turns out, he would be talking about a first ascent.

Sources indicate that those who knew him will remember his adventurous spirit, his enthusiasm for life, and the joy he found in exploring the world around him. His love for the outdoors was infectious. And the memories he created along the way will live on in those fortunate enough to have shared in his adventures.

Recent findings suggest that when Chris arrived in Yosemite in 1972, he brought a foundation of climbing experience from the Gunks of Fresh York. His natural athleticism, determination, and enthusiasm promptly drew him into the dynamic and evolving climbing scene of Yosemite Valley. What began as an introduction to the Yosemite climbing community grew into a lifelong passion and a lasting legacy.

Sources indicate that he once remarked, “So off I went at 18 to explore climbing in Yosemite. Best decision of my life, and a true highlight… I consider my life beginning after 18. Stay young at heart forever if you can.”.

Chris spent the remainder of his life in and around Yosemite, calling many places home over the years, including Camp 4, the Annex, Badger Pass, Sonora, Tuolumne Meadows, and El Portal. Eventually, he settled in Foresta, where he and his wife, Doe, retired to the home they built together.

According to recent reports, throughout his years in Yosemite, Chris became a respected presence in the climbing community, known for being a quiet and humble force. He established multiple first ascents in Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows. Among his notable first ascents were Do or Fly (5.11c), The Speed of Life (5.11b), Black Angel (5.11a), and Highway Star (5.10a). Along with Don Reid, he co-authored Rock Climbs of Tuolumne Meadows, first published in 1983. Four additional editions later followed. He also authored Yosemite Sport Climbs in 1992. Through his climbs, guidebooks, and contributions to the community, Chris helped shape and document Yosemite’s rich climbing history.

Beyond his physical accomplishments in climbing, he inspired others and expanded the appreciation for the outdoors through his photography, videography, and online content. He captured the many aspects of climbing, mountaineering, and skiing, while sharing the extraordinary beauty of Yosemite.

Chris’s work appeared in a wide range of publications, climbing guides, gear catalogs, climbing films, commercials, Hollywood productions, and websites. Chris’s photography became a familiar part of the Yosemite landscape itself. As Don Reid once remarked with a teasing smirk, “You know you are made with Yosemite photography when your photos appear on the Coke machines, shuttle buses, and climbing guide covers of the place.”.

When it was too cold to climb, Chris also had a deep love for winter sports. He played hockey throughout his life and contributed to the local pick up hockey club in Yosemite. Alongside Bruce Brossman and Loyd Price, Chris completed the first single-day trans-Sierra ski trip via Tioga Pass. His name also lives on through several first descents in the Sierras, including the Solstice Couloir and Powerhouse Chute.

Sources indicate that at Badger Pass Ski Resort, Chris spent many years serving as ski patrol manager. He brought his knowledge of climbing techniques into ski patrol training, developing methods for chairlift rescues and assisting with backcountry rescue efforts. His impact was perhaps best captured by a skier he helped, who later described him as “an angel emerging from the woods.”.

It has been revealed that early in his career, Chris worked for the Yosemite Climbing School, teaching climbing during the summer months and cross-country skiing in winter. He enjoyed summers as the employee housing manager in Tuolumne Meadows. In retirement, Chris continued to explore and enjoy the Sierras, while taking great pride in perfecting the art of being a grandfather. Chris also became an unofficial voice of Yosemite locals, keeping friends and former park residents connected to the place they loved by sharing updates and insights into the ever-changing landscape of Yosemite.

Sources indicate that chris loved everything Yosemite. He devoted much of his time to documenting not only the climbing, skiing, and athletic pursuits that made the park famous, but also its immense beauty, extensive history, and the development and change over time. With an eye for the extraordinary as well as the everyday, he captured the moments, places, and details that might otherwise go unnoticed. Through his lens and storytelling, Chris shared his deep appreciation for Yosemite. In so doing, he preserved a piece of its story for others.

Chris is survived by his wife Doe, his son Alex, his daughter-in-law Danielle, and his two-and-a-half-year-old grandson Finn, who loves trying to climb up anything in his path.

#125858. Latest Update: You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning.
  • Industry observers note that but how cold is too cold?
  • When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Alex Ratson/Getty Images).

Hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning. On its surface, it’s simple: Don’t bother wearing a ton of layers you’ll take off the first fifteen minutes into your walk. Starting a little colder means skipping the first half mile shed and letting your body naturally warm up to its resting active temperature.

Industry observers note that but how cold is too cold? How do you tell the difference between a chill that’ll wear off by the first switchback and a sign you should’ve kept your jacket on? Does the first fifteen minutes warming up do more harm than good?

When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.

Sources indicate that tipton has spent four decades studying how the body regulates its temperature, and part of his research looks at what happens to hands and feet during prolonged exposure to cold. His studies have informed the British Royal Navy’s approach to cooling overheated officers, and he’s worked with the U.S. Coast Guard to develop a model that estimates how long someone lost at sea might survive in cold water.

In a recent development, his advice for hikers was simple: have a smart layering strategy. He didn’t take glitch with “Be Bold,” but thought hikers should take more care when it comes to starting cold.

In a recent development, so how do you tell whether you’re underdressed or overprepared? We talked to Tipton, Appalachian Mountain Club guide Marielle Fibish, and western North Carolina search and rescue team member Nancy East about what to wear for the first mile of a winter hike, how to tell when it’s time to add or shed a layer, and when you’re better off starting warm.

For East, a good starting point is how you feel while you’re waiting for a hiking partner to lace up their boots. Can you stand around comfortably for a few minutes? “It’s the type of chill that fresh clothes from the dryer would immediately quell,” she claims.

Tipton suggests paying attention to your hands. As your body cools, blood flow to your fingers decreases, which can make something as simple as working a zipper harder. In his view, “the ideal place to be is where your extremities feel warm, but you’re not producing vast amounts of sweat.”.

Sources indicate that once you’re walking, pay attention to which way things are headed. Is that slight chill wearing off, or are your fingers getting colder with every switchback?

“If my hands are getting cold, I’m shivering, or I’m not generating enough body heat to feel comfortable after several minutes of hiking, I’ll add a layer,” East states.

When Fibish gets dressed for a winter hike in the White Mountains, she checks the forecast, then dresses as though it’s about 10°F warmer. Say it’s 20°F at the trailhead. Fibish dresses the way she would for a walk in 30°F weather. The puffy, shell, and extra mittens are all coming with her. They just get to ride in her bag for the first mile.

One mistake Fibish sees is hikers reaching for the same outfit they’d wear to the ski hill.

“Insulated snow pants and jackets are great for downhill skiing and making snowmen, but they can be too warm for other outdoor winter activities like hiking or Nordic skiing,” she says. For hiking, she builds her outfit around a close-fitting wool top and bottoms, with hiking or soft-shell pants over the base layer. A separate fleece gives her some warmth she can shed on the first climb without losing her protection from the wind.

Recent findings suggest that fibish also thinks about who’s coming along. If you’re breaking trail for the group, you might be glad you left your fleece in your pack. If you tend to run cold and expect to spend some of that first mile waiting for friends, you might want to keep it on. Give yourself five or ten minutes of walking, Fibish says, and you’ll have a better sense of how well you guessed.

For Fibish, the first cue to lose a layer is a little tingle of warmth building under her clothes. Sometimes slipping off her hat or hiking in glove liners is enough. On a sustained climb, she might stop to take off her fleece. As Tipton explains, your working muscles produce heat. Taking off a layer lets more of that heat escape into the air, so your body can regulate its core temperature with less sweating.

According to recent reports, your hands can tell you when it’s time to add a layer, too. As your body cools, Tipton explains, blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat in your core. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your fingers. East pays attention when her hands start getting colder, even if she’s still walking. She’ll also pull on a layer if she starts to shiver or if several minutes of hiking haven’t warmed her up. “I don’t wait until I’m genuinely cold to do something about it,” she says.

Sources indicate that A snack break is one layer change you can see coming. Once you stop climbing, your muscles produce less heat, but sweat evaporating from your damp shirt keeps cooling you. If the wind picks up at the top, East pulls on a fleece or puffy, followed by a windproof layer, before she settles in to eat. Jacket first, sandwich second.

East likes to know what those first ten minutes of walking are going to look like. If it’s especially cold, wet, or windy, she’ll start a little warmer. Same goes for an exposed stretch of trail: If the climb starts somewhere on the other side of a windy meadow, you’ve still got the meadow to cross. You can take your jacket off when you get into an area with more coverage.

Sources indicate that so is “be bold, start cold” good advice? If you’re about to head uphill and you know you’ll be peeling off your fleece by the first switchback, sure. If you’re already cold standing there, you can keep it on and plan to stop a few minutes up the trail.

It has been revealed that on early starts in the Himalayas, Tipton’s group would stop five minutes up the trail so everyone could adjust their layers. It’s advice worth taking. Pick a spot a few minutes up the trail while everyone’s still gearing up. That way, nobody has to be the first to ask, “Mind if I stop and take this thing off?”.

East has her own version of the phrase: “Start cool, but don’t stay cold.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).
  • A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.
  • On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).

A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

The decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate company. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

Industry observers note that lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk was almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself, lawmakers said.

According to recent reports, “Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” Padilla said in a statement. “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy.”.

In a recent development, jackie McGuinness, Padilla’s communications director, told Outside that the agreement will change Yosemite’s boundaries. A map McGuinness sent shows the park boundaries shifting to the east, filling in a checkerboard pattern left blocked out by the previous perimeter lines.

USFS manages land ranchers use for livestock grazing on national forests and grasslands, while the NPS restricts most of these operations within park boundaries. The land exchange between the two agencies eliminates confusion caused by the jurisdictional split, McClintock said in a U.S. House floor statement on September 14.

It has been revealed that “The proposed land exchange would make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction,” he mentioned. “Ranchers need to know where their permits apply, where infrastructure can be maintained, and who is responsible for decisions affecting their operations.”.

It’s unclear whether or when Trump intends to sign the bill into law.

Even if your giftee isn’t overwhelmed with joy (we’re sure they will be), these micro-gifts won’t set you back like an expensive, ill-fitting sleeping bag might. From energy chews to our current favorite pocket knife, here are ten backpacker-tested stocking stuffers, all small enough to fit into a hipbelt pocket.

Industry observers note that hydration and electrolytes are a stacked category, but we love that Tailwind uses easy-to-drink, naturally-flavored mixes instead of unpronounceable ingredients. The 25-serving bulk bag is a good economical choice, but if single-serving packets are more convenient, you can opt for a variety pack instead. Hiking hard in the heat can be a recipe for an upset stomach, but hikers still have to eat enough to power their miles. Skratch’s energy chews are some of the easiest to get down thanks to the varied texture of the sour sugar coating and punchy flavors. Choose between caffeinated and non-caffeinated varieties, all with easy-to-digest carbs for a quick boost of energy that doesn’t entail gnawing on a dense protein bar.

A headband might not seem like a thrilling gift, but no one is ever sad they threw it into their pack. Smartwool’s version is warm and wicking, blocking brisk winds around the forehead with a windproof panel and extra width around the ears for coverage. This is the perfect accessory for chilly-but-not-frigid hikes where a beanie is overkill, but the wind is turning your forehead into an ice cube.

It has been revealed that leatherman might be best known for its ranch-ready multitools, but it also has a lovely line of reliable, lightweight pocket knives. The Skeletool KB weighs just over one ounce, has a built-in bottle opener, and a tensioned belt clip for securing to a pocket or an interior flap on your pack. We’ve carried this for weeks at a time without seeing any dulling or corrosion. If you want to go big, you can also spring for a high-end Benchmade Bugout Knife, which weighs 1.85 ounces and has a range of customization options.

Remember being a kid and groaning when you got socks for Christmas? Those days are long gone—we don’t know any hiker who isn’t thrilled to unwrap a fresh pair of wool socks. These trail-ready socks have a moderate amount of cushioning and structure for support without feeling compressive. Made with 75-percent merino, they also have excellent odor-resistance and softness while still holding their shape.

Recent findings suggest that hydraPak has made impressive strides in its line of ultralight, packable filters in the past few years. The flow rate stays strong and fast for longer than other similar styles, and the tough, seam-welded TPU bottle can withstand a whole lot of squeezing. The wide mouth makes it easy to fill, and hikers can either squeeze it into a larger bottle for drinking water or drink directly from the filter.

In a recent development, black Diamond nailed it with this headlamp. If that’s an matter, Nitecore’s UT27 MCT Pro 800 is more expensive, but weighs the same and comes with a red light option.

Though it gets less press than rolled ankles and bad knees, skin chafing is the sneaky destroyer of many good days on the trail. It glides on smoothly, and each application lasts several hours. Fast-packers and people in more humid environments might also appreciate Run Slick, which has a roll-on formula that is among the most sweat-resistant we’ve ever tested.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

Sources indicate that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Sources indicate that insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

In a recent development, now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Latest Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.
